title: Nightingale edge egress onramp discovery
summary: Initial VPC onramp and egress controls discussion for a private Redwood deployment. Customer wants private endpoints + strict egress controls from EU regions to US analytics; discussed peering options, transit gateway, partner interconnect, NAT vs egress proxy, KMS, audit logs, and pilot sizing. Action items to share secure deployment checklist, region availability map, and a bandwidth test plan.
topics: VPC peering vs Private Link/private endpoints
Security: KMS, SOC2, audit logs, SSO
action_items: Ava: Share Redwood private deployment checklist and SOC2 summary by 2026-06-05
Devon: Draft network diagram options (VPC peering, TGW, PrivateLink) by 2026-06-08
Rahul: Provide expected token throughput and estimations for pilot by 2026-06-06
next_steps: Schedule technical pilot kickoff with Nightingale infra team week of 2026-06-15
Run small bandwidth/latency test from Nightingale EU region to Redwood staging (Devon to provide test script)
Follow up with security pack and architecture deck
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-03
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Devon Li (Redwood SE), Kara Thompson (Cloud Architect), Rahul Patel (SRE), Marta Lopez (Security Lead)
---
[00:00] Ava: hey everybody, thanks for joining. im ava with Redwood, im the account lead. quick roll call please
[00:07] Kara: hey kara here from nightingale, cloud arch.
[00:09] Rahul: rahul, sres.
[00:11] Marta: marta, security.
[00:13] Devon: devon, solutions engineer, i'll be walking through network options.
[00:16] Ava: awesome. goal today: understand your onramp constraints — private endpoints, peering, egress policy, regions — and map a pilot.
[00:25] Kara: high level, we need Redwood in a private deployment. Our product processes PHI-adjacent telemetry, we need EU data stay in eu, but analytics can go to us w/ controlled egress. looking for options for private endpoints or peering into our aws account.
[00:40] Devon: got it. two high-level paths we typically see: VPC peering/TGW style where you peer the customer VPC to Redwood's private VPCs, or private endpoint / private link style where you create endpoints in customer subnets that talk into our infra. both have tradeoffs for routing and egress.
[00:56] Rahul: latency and throughput are big for us. peak token generation can spike, and we have strict egress allowlists. we also use a transit gateway already for centralized egress via proxy.
[01:12] Marta: compliance is key: SOC2, full audit logs, customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for encrypting at rest. also we need to ensure that any metadata that leaves eu is minimized.
[01:23] Ava: understood. quick question — are you planning to host in a specific cloud region? eu-west-1 primarily?
[01:29] Kara: yes, primary eu-west-1, but we might need eu-central-1 for redundancy. can you confirm which regions Redwood private is available in and whether private endpoints are supported there?
[01:39] Devon: we support private deployments in eu-west-1 and eu-central-1 in our private offering, though some deployment modes may require slightly different configs. i'll include a region availability map. private endpoints are supported but implementation differs by cloud.
[01:51] Speaker 1: mm-hmm
[01:52] Rahul: tell me more about egress control. we have a central egress proxy that only allows outbound to a small bucket of analytics partners in the us. can the traffic from Redwood egress through our proxy or do you require direct internet?
[02:06] Devon: we can route egress through customer-managed transit gateway or via private peering; the key is the plumb — if you want to funnel everything through your centralized egress, we recommend TGW peering + route table controls so our nodes send outbound to your proxy. alternatively, PrivateLink tends to originate connections from customer side which makes allowlisting easier sometimes.
[02:25] Kara: any differences in NAT behavior? we saw differences last time with a vendor where SNAT changed source IPs and messed with our allowlist.
[02:33] Devon: good callout — with TGW peering the source IPs can be preserved if you handle routing without NAT. if we're crossing accounts and using older peering methods NAT might occur. PrivateLink usually preserves customer source since the connection is inbound to the endpoint from your VPC. i'll add exact packet flow diagrams.
[02:50] Marta: what about private IPs for callbacks? our data pipelines call back to an internal endpoint when jobs finish. do you support outbound webhooks to private IPs?
[02:59] Devon: yes, we support outbound calls to private destinations if routed through your transit. the pattern is: service invokes webhook, traffic egresses through your TGW and hits your private targets. we do have an option to use a proxy inside your VPC that receives traffic and then forwards internally.
[03:13] Rahul: are you able to support forced-tls mutual authentication for control plane? we need mTLS between our control plane and yours for some endpoints.
[03:21] Ava: we have mTLS for some control channels; for private deployments customers can bring a cert bundle. we'll confirm exact endpoints that support mTLS.
[03:29] Kara: also curious about peformance — what are typical latency numbers for requests inside same region vs cross-region?
[03:36] Devon: inside same region you can expect p50 around 30-60ms for small prompts on optimized models; p95 will depend on model size and batching. cross-region to us-east will add network latency; we can quantify during the pilot.
[03:50] Marta: we need to keep logs in eu for at least 7 years per internal policy. does Redwood support log retention in customer-controlled storage?
[03:59] Devon: yes, audit logs can be shipped to your S3/GCS bucket in eu, or you can ingest via our logging connector. customer-managed retention is supported in private deployments.
[04:10] Rahul: bandwidth — our uplink to our interconnect is 10Gb. what kind of burst behavior can we expect? can you provide expected token/sec to bandwidth mapping?
[04:21] Devon: we'll do a capacity estimate; for an LLM throughput estimate we typically provide tokens/sec per GPU and then map to bytes. i'll include a bandwidth test script for you to run.
[04:31] Kara: network architecture options — can you sketch three patterns? peering, private endpoint, and hybrid?
[04:36] Devon: sure. pattern A: direct VPC peering/TGW where Redwood nodes are part of a private network peered into your landing accounts (good for centralized routing). pattern B: customer private endpoints mapping to Redwood control plane (good for strict allowlists). pattern C: hybrid — PrivateLink for control plane + peered data plane for high throughput. i'll share diagrams.
[04:59] Ava: sounds like next step is we'll send the checklist and a proposed pilot design; Rahul can share traffic profile. Marta will review compliance pack.
[05:06] Kara: quick note on region egress — we want to avoid any callouts to us regions for PII metadata. is there any metadata your control plane will send back to us-east?
[05:18] Devon: default control plane telemetry can be configured to stay in-region for private deployments; some meta-metrics used for platform health may be optional. we'll mark them and provide opt-out.
[05:28] Speaker 2: uh-huh
[05:30] Rahul: what about key management — can we bring our KMS? we want envelope encryption under our key.
[05:37] Ava: yes, BYOK is supported for private deployments; we integrate with customer KMS or HSM — need to confirm exact key policies.
[05:43] Marta: do you have attestations for HSM FIPS compliance?
[05:47] Devon: we use cloud KMS providers for the default path; for HSM-level keys we support customer-managed HSMs via our private deployment integrations — will share details.
[05:56] Kara: timeline — we'd like pilot in 3 weeks, full prod in 3 months if pilot ok.
[06:01] Ava: that's reasonable. our pilot usually runs 2-4 weeks. we'll scope minimal footprint.
[06:06] Rahul: any limitations around egress ports? our proxy only allows 443 and 5222 for legacy.
[06:11] Devon: 443 is primary; we do not require 5222. certain telemetry ports are optional. we'll provide a firewall egress matrix.
[06:20] Kara: can you support dedicated capacity later? we may move to dedicated GPUs once throughput steady.
[06:25] Ava: yes Dedicated or Dedicated-reserved capacity is supported; we'll outline transition steps and how routing changes.
[06:31] Marta: audit trail — need per-request tracing and token-level cost hooks for billing reconciliation. can you provide that?
[06:39] Devon: per-request trace ids and usage logs are available and can be delivered to your logging bucket; token-level breakdowns also possible, though we may need to filter PII from logs.
[06:50] Speaker 3: mm
[06:52] Rahul: do you have experience with a hub-and-spoke TGW model where multiple teams route through the same transit? we have multiple business units and would like standardization.
[06:58] Devon: yes, common pattern is TGW hub in the security account; Redwood peered into a central egress account. we'll show route table proposals that avoid asymmetric routing.
[07:09] Kara: regarding private endpoints, will you require any changes to our VPC CIDR ranges? we have a lot of existing overlaps.
[07:17] Devon: CIDR overlap can block peering. PrivateLink is often better when overlaps exist because it uses ENIs and does not require unique CIDR ranges. hybrid also helps.
[07:29] Marta: any forensic access for us? e.g. can we pull raw request payloads on demand?
[07:36] Ava: we can provide redacted payload access and raw payloads under strict controls; will need a data access agreement.
[07:44] Rahul: one weird thing — our compliance team requires that outbound DNS for these services be resolvable only by our own DNS forwarders. can we set that up with PrivateLink?
[07:54] Devon: yes, you can use zone-association and private zones that resolve endpoints to private ips, or use endpoint-specific DNS entries. we'll provide DNS setup docs.
[08:04] Kara: latency targets for pilot — we want p95 < 300ms for small requests. think that's doable?
[08:11] Devon: likely yes inside-region with right instance types and batching configs; we'll set up benchmarks during pilot.
[08:17] Speaker 4: okay
[08:18] Ava: ok let's do a short demo of one diagram — devon?
[08:22] Devon: shared screen (descriptive) pattern A: TGW peering, Redwood nodes in our private subnet, route tables in your security account, control plane endpoints via PrivateLink. Pattern C: hybrid, data plane peered, control plane via private endpoints.
[08:40] Kara: in hybrid, how do you manage failover if peering goes down?
[08:44] Devon: we have automated fallback policies that can reroute to a hosted fallback region, but that would cross boundaries; for strict compliance you'd set up multi-region redundant private deployments.
[08:57] Marta: fallback must be explicit and manual for us — no automatic cross-border failover.
[09:02] Ava: noted — manual failover option exists. we'll make that explicit in the runbook.
[09:07] Rahul: about monitoring — do you export metrics to Prometheus in our monitoring account?
[09:13] Devon: yes, we can export Prometheus metrics via remote write into your monitoring stack, or push logs to your metrics account.
[09:20] Kara: any cost implications for peering vs endpoint?
[09:24] Ava: generally endpoints (PrivateLink) have per-GB data processing charges plus ENI costs; peering/TGW has data transfer charges. we'll provide a cost comparison for your targeted throughput.
[09:36] Kara: great. can we get a sample pricing for pilot (4 weeks) for 2 GPUs?
[09:41] Ava: yes we'll send a pilot quote.
[09:43] Rahul: about the test script — what does it exercise?
[09:46] Devon: it hits our staging using the private path, measures latency, records throughput, and validates source ip preservation. i'll include auth tokens and sample payloads but redact pII.
[09:58] Mara: (sic) marta: can you also confirm data deletion processes post-pilot? we need certs.
[10:04] Ava: yes data deletion and retention policies are in the compliance pack; we can provide deletion certs after pilot completion.
[10:10] Kara: anything else?
[10:12] Rahul: one more — how do you handle KV cache and warmup across nodes? if we have cache locality needs can we pin models to dedicated pools?
[10:21] Devon: yes, you can pin models to dedicated capacity and we manage KV cache affinity. that helps warm-start latency.
[10:28] Ava: cool. recap: we'll send private dep checklist, SOC2 summary, region map, diagram options, pilot quote, and the test script. Rahul to share throughput numbers. schedule pilot kickoff.
[10:39] Kara: sounds good. thanks all.
[10:41] Ava: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with meeting notes and next steps.
---
Post-meeting notes (auto section):
- Tone: collaborative, security-focused.
- Pilot scope: small footprint in eu-west-1, PrivateLink for control plane, TGW peering for data plane (recommended), optional hosted fallback disabled by default.
- Risks: CIDR overlap, strict no-cross-border automatic failover, requirement for BYOK/HSM details.
- Artifacts to share: architecture deck, region availability map, compliance pack (SOC2), pilot quote, bandwidth test script.
End of transcript.
